### Analysis of Diode States
Given: $V_m = 9\text{ V}$, $V_1 = 5\text{ V}$, $V_2 = 6\text{ V}$.
Let the diodes be ideal. The cathodes of both diodes are connected to the output $V_0$, while their anodes are connected to fixed DC voltages $V_1 = 5\text{ V}$ and $V_2 = 6\text{ V}$ respectively.
* A diode conducts when its anode voltage is greater than or equal to its cathode voltage ($V_{\text{anode}} \ge V_{\text{cathode}}$).
* Since $V_1 = 5\text{ V}$ and $V_2 = 6\text{ V}$, the diode with the higher anode potential tends to pull the output $V_0$ up, turning off the other diode.
* Comparing the fixed DC biases, $V_2 = 6\text{ V} > V_1 = 5\text{ V}$, so the diode connected to $V_2$ will conduct and hold the output at $6\text{ V}$ as long as the input $v_i$ allows.

### Output Waveform $V_0$
The input $v_i$ varies sinusoidally between $+9\text{ V}$ and $-9\text{ V}$. 
* When $v_i$ is below $6\text{ V}$, the diode connected to $V_2$ is forward-biased, clipping the output at **$V_0 = 6\text{ V}$**.
* When $v_i$ exceeds $6\text{ V}$ (up to its peak of $9\text{ V}$), the output follows the input waveform **$V_0 = v_i$**.

Therefore, the output waveform $V_0$ is clipped at $6\text{ V}$ for all input values below $6\text{ V}$, and follows $v_i$ from $6\text{ V}$ to $9\text{ V}$.
proTip: For clipper/clamper circuits with ideal diodes, always determine which diode conducts by comparing the node voltages at transition instants.
